{{Short description|Type of catenary curve}}

[[File:St Louis night expblend cropped.jpg|350px|thumb|The [[Gateway Arch]] is a weighted catenary: thick at the bottom, thin at the top.|alt=]]

A '''weighted catenary''' (also '''flattened catenary''', was defined by [[William Rankine]] as '''transformed catenary'''<ref>{{cite journal|last=Osserman |first=Robert |title=Mathematics of the Gateway Arch |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201002/rtx100200220p.pdf |date=February 2010 |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |issn=0002-9920 |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=220–229 }}</ref> and thus sometimes called '''Rankine curve'''<ref name="=">{{cite web |last1=Andrue |first1=Mario |title=The arches of the facade of the Palau Güell. Hyphotesis about its conformation |url=https://fundacionantoniogaudi.org/Publicaciones/the-arches-of-the-facade-of-the-palau-guell.pdf |website=fundacionantoniogaudi.org |publisher=Antonio Gaudi Foundation |access-date=5 January 2024 |date=2020}}</ref>) is a [[catenary]] curve, but of a special form: while a catenary is the curve formed by a chain under its own weight, a weighted catenary is the curve formed if the chain's weight is not consistent along its length. Formally, a "regular" catenary has the equation

:<math>y = a \, \cosh \left(\frac{x}{a}\right) = \frac{a\left(e^\frac{x}{a} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)}{2}</math>

for a given value of ''a''. A ''weighted catenary'' has the equation

:<math>y = b \, \cosh \left(\frac{x}{a}\right) = \frac{b\left(e^\frac{x}{a} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)}{2}</math>

and now ''two'' constants enter: ''a'' and ''b''.

==Significance==

[[File:Kette Kettenkurve Catenary 2008 PD.JPG|right|300px|thumb|A hanging [[chain]] is a regular [[catenary]] &mdash; and is not weighted.]]

A freestanding [[catenary arch]] has a uniform thickness. However, if

# the arch is not of uniform thickness,<ref name="https://www.ams.org/notices/201002/rtx100200220p.pdf">{{cite web | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201002/rtx100200220p.pdf | title=Mathematics of the Gateway Arch | publisher=Notices of the AMS | date=February 2010 | author=Robert Osserman}}</ref>
# the arch supports more than its own weight,<ref name="blogspot.co.uk">Re-review: Catenary and Parabola: [http://arch-re-review.blogspot.co.uk/2010/09/catenary-and-parabola.html Re-review: Catenary and Parabola], accessdate: April 13, 2017</ref>
# or if gravity varies,<ref name="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/29247/catenary-curve-under-non-uniform-gravitational-field">MathOverflow: [https://mathoverflow.net/questions/29247/catenary-curve-under-non-uniform-gravitational-field classical mechanics - Catenary curve under non-uniform gravitational field - MathOverflow], accessdate: April 13, 2017</ref>

it becomes more complex. A weighted catenary is needed.

The [[aspect ratio]] of a weighted catenary (or other curve) describes a rectangular frame containing the selected fragment of the curve theoretically continuing to the infinity. <ref name="techtarget.com">Definition from WhatIs.com: [http://whatis.techtarget.com/definition/aspect-ratio What is aspect ratio? - Definition from WhatIs.com], accessdate: April 13, 2017</ref><ref name="How the Gateway Arch Got its Shape">{{cite web | url=http://www.msri.org/people/staff/osserman/papers/NNJ_v12n2_Osserman_pp167-189.pdf | title=How the Gateway Arch Got its Shape | publisher=Nexus Network Journal | date=2010 | accessdate=13 April 2017 | author=Robert Osserman}}</ref>

==Examples==

The [[Gateway Arch]] in the American city of [[St. Louis]], [[Missouri]], is the most famous example of a weighted catenary.{{Citation needed|date=November 2024}}

[[Simple suspension bridge]]s use weighted catenaries.<ref name="How the Gateway Arch Got its Shape" />
